latin.232: GAR. Etenim 1. non unum idemque sunt, quorum unum idem homo eodem tempore velle potest, & alterum nolle. At ita habet in hac causa. Adamus enim de fructu interdicto comedens, volebat violare Dei praeceptum, sed nolebat justitiam suam & praerogativas amittere.
latin.233: PLAC. Utraque propositio est falsa; Major quidem; potest enim unum idemque homo idem eodem tempore ob diversas rationes velle & nolle. Idque evenit frequenter: inde haesitatio, & deliberatio, & pugna nonnunquam inter cogitationes volitionesque nostras. Deinde est voluntas rectae rationi conformis, & est voluntas errans & rectae rationi repugnans: haec secum ipsa nonnunquam pugnat. Denique nemo vult malum qua malum formaliter, hoc est, quatenus est privatio boni. Itaque mirum videri non debet, si Adamus privationem justitiae formaliter non voluit. Ita enim peccatum suum voluisset sub ratione mali. Quod etiam in Minore ait, Adamum voluisse violare Dei praeceptum, materialiter tantum ut sic loquar, non formaliter, verum est. Voluit enim id quod erat violatio praecepti Dei, sed non sub ratione violationis praecepti divini, sed sub ratione magnae cujusdam bonitatis sibi falso apparentis. Quod si formaliter volebat violare Dei praeceptum, & tamen nolebat justitiam suam amittere, stultus erat, putans separari posse, quae separari nullo modo poterant.
latin.234: GAR. 2. Ea non sunt unum & idem, quae reapse possunt separari. Atqui potest aliquis violare legem, qui tamen propterea justitia sua habituali actu non privabitur, quod patet exemplo fidelium, qui subinde peccant, nec tamen privantur ea justitia, quam Deus spiritu suo in ipsorum cordibus operatus est.
latin.235: PLAC. Conclusionem non expressit: haud enim ex duabus illis praemissis concludi potest id quod ei probandum incumbebat. Agitur enim non de omni violatione legis, sed de tali, nempe prima illa Adami, nec de qualibet privatione justitiae, sed de privatione justitiae qua praeditus erat ante lapsum Adamus. De hac enim violatione & privatione intelligenda est argumenti mei propositio minor. Aut igitur universalem esse oportebat Viri Docti Minorem, aut nominatim de illa privatione & violatione intelligi. Neutrum cum sit factum, nihil potest concludi mihi repugnans. Deinde simili argumento possent infinitae propositiones verissimae refelli, etiam ista, homo est animal. Nam ea non sunt unum & idem quae reapse possunt separari. Atqui potest aliquid esse animal, nec tamen esse homo.
latin.236: Distinguo tamen ut supra justitiae privationem. Est enim privatio justitiae actualis & privatio justitiae habitualis: illa est violatio legis actualis, haec habitualis. Sed rursus distinguenda est justitia: accipi enim potest vel forensi significatione vel morali. Utraque rursus vel est legalis vel evangelica. Justitia forensis legalis, quia consistit in perfecta totius vitae conformitate cum lege, vel unica legis violatione amittitur. Una enim ad condemnationem sufficit. Evangelicae dispar est ratio: cum enim in remissione peccatorum consistat, palam est violationem legis non excludere remissionem peccati. Justitia vero morali sensu accepta opponitur, ut dixi, violationi legis, hoc est, injustitiae, actualis quidem actuali, habitualis vero habituali. Sed quaeritur an violatio actualis inducat necessario privationem justitiae habitualis? Distinctione opus est. Dispar enim est ratio habitus justitiae naturalis seu legalis, qualis ponitur esse in Adamo, & habitus justitiae supernaturalis seu evangelicae. Illa enim nec spem includit remissionis peccatorum, nec aliunde pendere videtur quam a facultate hominis naturali. Itaque violatione legis amittitur. Haec vero quia fidem ac spem remissionis peccatorum includit, & pendet ab alio principio quam humano, nempe a Spiritu regenerationis Sancto, & Decreto electionis, simplici legis violatione non excutitur. Est etiam violatio legis duplex: una est universalis a Deo ἀποστασία, seu mutatio finis ultimi, altera, particulare quodvis peccatum: Illa habitum justitiae delet, haec laedit quidem, at non destruit. Cum ergo justitia Adami legalis ac naturalis esset, ejusque peccatum universalis quaedam a Deo apostasia, seu finis ultimi mutatio, fieri non potuit, quin simul ac peccavit justitia privaretur, nec opus fuit, ut Deus judiciaria aliqua actione eum justitia privaret.
latin.237: GAR. 3. Denique sicut actus illi, quibus habitus comparatur, non sunt ipsa habitus acquisitio, sed ad eos consequitur acquisitio: ita etiam actus, quibus excutitur habitus, non sunt ipsa habitus privatio, sed ad eos consequitur illa privatio. Frustra ergo jactat Vir Doctus in Thesibus suis de statu hom. Lapsi ante Grat. Th. 24. Nos hoc ipso justitia privari, quod legem transgredimur, & hac ipsa mutatione, qua corruptio introducta est in Adamum, ab eodem expulsam esse justitiam. Etenim si intelligit transgressionem legis esse causam meritoriam privationis justitiae, facile agnoscimus. Si putat transgressionem legis & privationem justitiae nihil inter se differre omnino, non probamus: quia transgressio legis est actio, privatio justitiae passio est: at pati & agere plusquam verbis differunt: Et Deus animas hominum creat justitia originalis decoramento destitutas, qui tamen creando non facit legis praevaricatrices. Sic expulsio justitiae est antecedens ad corruptionem, & corruptio consequens ad expulsionem justitiae: antecedens autem & consequens, nonnihil differunt inter se, ut opinor: Et Deus hominem concessis creatione donis spoliavit, quem tamen non corrupit.
latin.238: PLAC. Aberrat etiam haec responsio ab argumenti mei propositione minore. Cum enim dixi, privationem justitiae esse violationem conditionis seu praecepti, id ita accipi debuit, ut privatio justitiae actualis esse intelligeretur violatio actualis, & privatio justitiae habitualis, violatio habitualis. Sed videtur habituale peccatum Vir Doctus nullo fere loco habere. Itaque non frustra est quod me jactasse dicit in Thesibus: quo verbo, seu jactationem seu jactantiam significet, cur uteretur quam ei ansam praebuerim non possum videre. Divisi autem quae conjunxit, hocque dilemmate sum usus. Si justitia sumitur sensu forensi, nonne ea privamur hoc ipso quod legem transgredimur? In hoc dilemmatis membro quid reprehendat, aut reprehendi possit, non intelligo. Sequitur alterum; Si sensu morali: Annon hac ipsa mutatione, qua corruptio contraria justitiae in Adamum introducta est, ab eodem expulsa est justitia, haud aliter quam obtenebratione aeris expellitur lumen, aut frigesactione calor? In his quoque verbis meis quid reprehendit? Si intelligo transgressionem legis esse causam meritoriam privationis justitiae facile agnoscit. Hoc vero si intelligerem mecum ipse pugnarem, qui hoc, de quo agitur, argumentum affero, ut probem privationem justitiae originalis non esse poenam proprie dictam. Certe transgressio legis injustitia seu privatio justitiae est; justitia, inquam, actualis si est actio vel actionis omissio, habitualis vero si est habitus: transgredimur enim legem non solum actione, sed etiam habitu. Si puto transgressionem legis & privationem justitiae nihil inter se differre omnino, non probat. Ego vero nihil aliud volo, quam ut propositio mea vera sit, sive attributum & subjectum nihil omnino differant, sive differant nonnihil. Nam propositiones, homo est animal, homo est risibilis, verae sunt, quamvis subjectum & attributum plusquam nominibus differant. Sed quomodo probat differre? transgressio, inquit, legis est actio. Omnisne transgressio? non habitualis, ut opinor, nec ea actualis, quae in omissione actionis consistit. Sed pergat. Privatio justitiae passio est. At modo distinguebat privationem in activam & passivam. Est-ne igitur privatio activa passio? non sit veri simile. Passiva quoque, estne passio? at dicitur respectu Dei qui omnis passionis est expers. Certe privatio formaliter non est passio, sed reducitur ad praedicamentum formae seu termini cujus est negatio. Hoc docent omnes Logici. Passio non minus quam actio transit; Privatio vero permanet, etiam postquam actio & passio desierunt esse. Passio formaliter est ens reale, & per se est in praedicamento, privatio nec formaliter est ens sed negatio potius, nec in praedicamento nisi reductive. Mitto alias differentias inter passionem & privationem. Addo posita actione, cujus terminus sit accidens, poni necessario passionem; hancque ab illa non realiter differre, sed respectu tantum & ratione. Quod subjungit, Deus animas hominum creare justitiae originalis decoramento destitutas, qui tamen creando non facit legis praevaricatrices, illud quale sit considerari oportet. Nam creat quidem animas justitia privatas, sed sic tamen, ut hujus privationis autor non sit, eam ipsae contrahant a corpore. Alioquin enim eas, si privaret justitia, faceret injustas. Nam inter justum & injustum, sanctum & pollutum in subjecto capaci nullum est medium. Quid porro est, quod addit, Sic expulsio justitiae est antecedens ad corruptionem, & corruptio consequens ad expulsionem justitiae? Primo enim expulsio justitiae, praesupponit justitiam praeexistentem in subjecto unde expellitur. Non fuit autem originalis justitia nisi in solo Adamo. Ab eo igitur solo expulsa est. Deinde quis credat Deum ab homine justitiam expellere, ac propterea quod ab eo expulsa sit, ei irasci? Item Deum causam esse privationis justitiae, nec tamen esse causam corruptionis? Perinde enim est, ac si eum dicerem, qui tollit a corpore rectitudinem, non esse causam obliquitatis, aut qui tollit a corpore humano sanitatem, morbi causam non esse. Mihi quidem certe videtur nec corruptio moralis absque privatione justitiae, nec privatio justitiae absque corruptione morali consistere ullo modo, aut intelligi posse. Nam sive privative justitia & corruptio opponuntur, haec illius privatio est; sive contrarie, expellunt sese mutuo ex eodem subjecto capaci, & quidem immediate. Nullum enim medium concipi animo potest inter justitiam & injustitiam, virtutem & vitium, rectitudinem & obliquitatem &c. in subjecto capaci.

pass_a.232: GAR. For indeed 1. those things are not one and the same, of which a man can at the same time will the one and not-will the other. But so it stands in this case. For Adam, eating of the forbidden fruit, was willing to violate God's precept, but was unwilling to lose his justice and prerogatives.
pass_a.233: PLAC. Both propositions are false; the Major indeed; for one and the same man can at the same time, for diverse reasons, will and not-will the same thing. And that happens frequently: thence hesitation, and deliberation, and sometimes a fight among our thoughts and volitions. Next there is a will conformed to right reason, and there is an erring will and one that fights right reason: this sometimes fights with itself. Finally no one wills evil as evil formally, that is, insofar as it is privation of a good. And so it ought not seem strange if Adam did not formally will the privation of justice. For so he would have willed his sin under the aspect of evil. What he also says in the Minor, that Adam willed to violate God's precept, materialiter only (so to speak), not formaliter, is true. For he willed that which was a violation of God's precept, but not under the aspect of violation of the divine precept, but under the aspect of some great goodness falsely appearing to him. But if he formally willed to violate God's precept, and yet was unwilling to lose his justice, he was a fool, thinking those things could be separated which in no way could be separated.
pass_a.234: GAR. 2. Those things are not one and the same which in the thing itself can be separated. But someone can violate the law who nevertheless will not for that reason in act be deprived of his habitual justice, which is clear from the example of the faithful, who from time to time sin, and yet are not deprived of that justice which God by his Spirit has wrought in their hearts.
pass_a.235: PLAC. He did not express the conclusion: for from those two premises that which it fell to him to prove cannot be concluded. For it is not a matter of every violation of the law, but of such a one, namely that first of Adam, nor of any privation of justice you please, but of the privation of the justice with which Adam was endowed before the fall. For of this violation and privation the minor proposition of my argument is to be understood. Therefore either the Learned Man's Minor ought to have been universal, or to be understood namely of that privation and violation. Since neither has been done, nothing opposing me can be concluded. Next by a like argument countless most true propositions could be refuted, even this, man is an animal. For those things are not one and the same which in the thing itself can be separated. But something can be an animal and yet not be a man.
pass_a.236: Yet I distinguish, as above, the privation of justice. For there is privation of actual justice and privation of habitual justice: that is actual violation of the law, this habitual. But again justice is to be distinguished: for it can be taken either in a forensic signification or a moral. Each again is either legal or evangelical. Forensic legal justice, because it consists in perfect conformity of the whole life with the law, is lost even by a single violation of the law. For one suffices for condemnation. Of evangelical [justice] the reason is different: since it consists in remission of sins, it is plain that violation of the law does not exclude remission of sin. But justice taken in a moral sense is opposed, as I said, to violation of the law, that is, to injustice—actual indeed to actual, but habitual to habitual. But it is asked whether actual violation necessarily induces privation of habitual justice? Distinction is needed. For the reason of the habit of natural or legal justice, such as is supposed to be in Adam, and of the habit of supernatural or evangelical justice, is different. For that neither includes hope of remission of sins, nor seems to depend from elsewhere than from man's natural faculty. And so by violation of the law it is lost. But this, because it includes faith and hope of remission of sins, and depends on another principle than the human, namely on the Holy Spirit of regeneration and the Decree of election, is not shaken off by a simple violation of the law. There is also a twofold violation of the law: one is universal ἀποστασία from God, or change of the last end; the other, any particular sin: That deletes the habit of justice; this wounds indeed, but does not destroy. Since therefore Adam's justice was legal and natural, and his sin a certain universal apostasy from God, or change of the last end, it could not happen but that as soon as he sinned he was deprived of justice, nor was there need that God by some judicial action deprive him of justice.
pass_a.237: GAR. 3. Finally just as those acts by which a habit is acquired are not themselves the acquisition of the habit, but acquisition follows upon them: so also the acts by which a habit is shaken off are not themselves the privation of the habit, but that privation follows upon them. In vain therefore does the Learned Man boast in his Theses on the state of fallen man before Grace, Th. 24: that we are deprived of justice by this very [fact], that we transgress the law, and that by this very change by which corruption was introduced into Adam, justice was expelled from the same. For if he understands transgression of the law to be the meritorious cause of privation of justice, we easily grant it. If he thinks transgression of the law and privation of justice differ nothing at all between themselves, we do not approve: because transgression of the law is an action, privation of justice is a passion: but to suffer and to act differ more than in words: And God creates men's souls destitute of the ornament of original justice, who yet by creating does not make them transgressors of the law. So expulsion of justice is antecedent to corruption, and corruption consequent to expulsion of justice: but antecedent and consequent differ somewhat between themselves, as I suppose: And God stripped man of the gifts granted in creation, whom yet he did not corrupt.
pass_a.238: PLAC. This reply also wanders from the minor proposition of my argument. For when I said privation of justice is violation of the condition or precept, it ought to have been so taken that privation of actual justice would be understood as actual violation, and privation of habitual justice as habitual violation. But the Learned Man seems to give habitual sin almost no place. And so it is not for nothing that he says I boasted in the Theses: by which word, whether he means boasting or boastfulness, why he would use it I cannot see what handle I gave him. But I divided what he joined, and used this dilemma. If justice is taken in a forensic sense, are we not deprived of it by this very [fact] that we transgress the law? In this member of the dilemma what he reprehends, or what can be reprehended, I do not understand. The other follows; If in a moral sense: Is it not by this very change by which corruption contrary to justice was introduced into Adam that justice was expelled from the same, no otherwise than by darkening of the air light is expelled, or by cooling heat? In these words of mine too what does he reprehend? If I understand transgression of the law to be the meritorious cause of privation of justice he easily grants it. But if I understood that I would fight with myself, I who bring forward this argument under discussion in order to prove that privation of original justice is not punishment properly so called. Certainly transgression of the law is injustice or privation of justice; justice, I say, actual if it is an action or omission of an action, but habitual if it is a habit: for we transgress the law not only by action but also by habit. If I think transgression of the law and privation of justice differ nothing at all between themselves, he does not prove [his point]. But I want nothing else than that my proposition be true, whether attribute and subject differ nothing at all, or differ somewhat. For the propositions 'man is an animal,' 'man is risible,' are true, although subject and attribute differ more than in names. But how does he prove they differ? Transgression of the law, he says, is an action. Is every transgression? not the habitual, as I suppose, nor that actual which consists in omission of an action. But let him go on. Privation of justice is a passion. But just now he was distinguishing privation into active and passive. Is active privation therefore a passion? it would not be likely. Passive also—is it a passion? but it is said with respect to God who is void of every passion. Certainly privation formally is not a passion, but is reduced to the predicament of the form or term of which it is the negation. All the Logicians teach this. Passion no less than action passes; but Privation remains, even after action and passion have ceased to be. Passion formally is a real being, and per se is in a predicament; privation neither formally is a being but rather a negation, nor in a predicament except reductively. I pass over other differences between passion and privation. I add that given an action whose term is an accident, passion is necessarily posited; and that this does not differ from that really, but only in respect and reason. What he subjoins, that God creates men's souls destitute of the ornament of original justice, who yet by creating does not make them transgressors of the law—what that is like ought to be considered. For he indeed creates souls deprived of justice, but so nevertheless that he is not the author of this privation: they themselves contract it from the body. For otherwise if he deprived them of justice he would make them unjust. For between just and unjust, holy and polluted, in a capable subject there is no middle. What further is that which he adds, So expulsion of justice is antecedent to corruption, and corruption consequent to expulsion of justice? For first, expulsion of justice presupposes justice preexisting in the subject whence it is expelled. But original justice was not except in Adam alone. From him alone therefore was it expelled. Next who would believe that God expels justice from man, and because it has been expelled from him is angry at him? Likewise that God is the cause of privation of justice and yet is not the cause of corruption? For it is just as if I should say that he who takes straightness from a body is not the cause of crookedness, or he who takes health from a human body is not the cause of disease. To me indeed it certainly seems that neither moral corruption without privation of justice, nor privation of justice without moral corruption, can in any way consist or be understood. For whether privately justice and corruption are opposed, this is the privation of that; or contrariwise, they mutually expel each other from the same capable subject, and indeed immediately. For no middle can be conceived in the mind between justice and injustice, virtue and vice, straightness and crookedness, etc., in a capable subject.

232: Garissoles' first reason. Things are not one and the same if a man can at once will the one and refuse the other. So here: Adam, eating the forbidden fruit, meant to break God's command, yet did not mean to lose his righteousness and privileges.
233: Placeus. Both premises fail. On the major: one and the same person can, for different reasons, will and refuse the same thing at once—hence hesitation, deliberation, and the clash among our thoughts and choices. There is a will aligned with right reason and a will that errs against it; the erring will sometimes fights itself. No one formally wills evil as evil—as privation of a good—so it is no wonder Adam did not formally will the loss of righteousness; that would have been to will his sin under the aspect of evil.

What Garissoles says in the minor—that Adam willed to break the precept only materialiter, not formaliter—is right. Adam willed what was in fact a breach of God's command, but under the guise of some great apparent good, not under the aspect "breach of divine law." If he had formally meant to break the precept and yet refused to lose righteousness, he would have been a fool, imagining inseparable things could be parted.
234: Garissoles' second reason. Things that can really be separated are not one and the same. Someone may break the law and still not, in the act, lose habitual righteousness—as the faithful show, who sin from time to time yet keep the righteousness God works in their hearts by his Spirit.
235: Placeus. He never states the conclusion; those two premises cannot yield what he needs to prove. The question is not every law-breaking, but Adam's first; not any loss of righteousness, but the loss of the righteousness Adam had before the fall. My minor is about that breach and that loss. Garissoles' minor must either be universal or name that case; neither done, nothing against me follows.
The same pattern would overturn endless true propositions—even "man is an animal." Things that can really be separated are not identical; something can be an animal and yet not a man.
236: I still distinguish, as before, privation of righteousness: actual and habitual—actual law-breaking and habitual. Righteousness itself must be split again: forensic or moral; and each either legal or evangelical. Forensic legal righteousness is perfect lifelong conformity to the law, so a single breach loses it—one is enough for condemnation. Evangelical forensic righteousness rests on remission of sins, so breaking the law does not shut out forgiveness.

Moral righteousness stands opposite injustice—actual to actual, habitual to habitual. Does an actual breach necessarily strip habitual righteousness? Distinguish. Natural or legal habit (as in Adam) neither hopes for remission nor rests on anything but natural faculty, so law-breaking loses it. Supernatural or evangelical habit includes faith and hope of remission and hangs on the regenerating Spirit and the decree of election, so a mere breach does not shake it off.

Law-breaking itself is twofold: universal ἀποστασία from God—a change of the last end—or any particular sin. The first destroys the habit of righteousness; the second wounds it but does not wreck it. Adam's righteousness was legal and natural, and his sin a universal apostasy, a turn of the last end; so the moment he sinned he lost righteousness, and God needed no separate judicial act to strip him of it.
237: Garissoles' third reason. Acts that build a habit are not themselves the acquiring of the habit—acquisition follows them. Likewise acts that shake a habit off are not themselves the privation—privation follows them. So Placeus boasts in vain in his Theses on fallen man before grace (Th. 24): that we lose righteousness by the very fact that we break the law, and that the change which brought corruption into Adam itself expelled righteousness from him.

If he means law-breaking is the meritorious cause of losing righteousness, we grant it. If he thinks law-breaking and privation of righteousness differ not at all, we refuse: breaking the law is an action; privation is a passion; acting and suffering differ more than in words. God creates souls without the ornament of original righteousness yet does not, by creating, make them law-breakers. Expulsion of righteousness precedes corruption; corruption follows expulsion—antecedent and consequent differ. God stripped man of creation's gifts yet did not corrupt him.
238: Placeus. This answer also misses my minor. When I said privation of righteousness is breach of the condition or precept, I meant actual privation as actual breach, habitual privation as habitual breach. Garissoles scarcely allows habitual sin a place. Calling my Theses "boasting" I cannot see what handle I gave him. I split what he joined and used this dilemma.

If righteousness is forensic, do we not lose it by the very fact of breaking the law? I see nothing to fault there. If moral: was righteousness not expelled from Adam by the very change that introduced the contrary corruption—as darkening drives out light, or cooling heat? If he takes me to mean law-breaking is only the meritorious cause of privation, he grants it; were that all I meant I would contradict myself, since I argue that privation of original righteousness is not punishment properly so called. Law-breaking is injustice—privation of righteousness—actual if act or omission, habitual if habit; we break the law by habit as well as by act.

He does not prove they differ "not at all." I only need my proposition true whether subject and attribute are identical or differ somewhat—as "man is an animal" and "man is risible" remain true though subject and attribute differ more than in names. "Law-breaking is an action"—every breach? Not habitual; nor actual omission. He says privation is a passion, yet had just split privation into active and passive. Is active privation a passion? Unlikely. Is "passive" a passion when said of God, who suffers nothing? Formally privation is not passion but reduces to the predicament of the form it negates—so the logicians. Passion passes with action; privation remains. Passion is a real being in a predicament; privation is rather a negation, in a predicament only reductively.

As for God creating souls bare of original righteousness without making them transgressors: he creates them without righteousness, yet is not author of that privation—they contract it from the body; else by stripping them he would make them unjust, and in a capable subject there is no middle between just and unjust. "Expulsion precedes corruption"? Expulsion presupposes righteousness already in the subject; original righteousness was only in Adam, so only from him was it expelled. Who believes God expels righteousness and then is angry because it is gone—or causes the privation yet not the corruption? That is like saying who takes straightness from a body does not cause crookedness, or who takes health does not cause disease. Moral corruption and privation of righteousness cannot stand or be thought apart. Whether they oppose privatively or contrarily, they drive each other out of the same capable subject at once; there is no middle between justice and injustice, virtue and vice, straight and crooked, in a capable subject.
